settings.question: How do I use KAMI?
settings.answer: Four drops onto the scalp each night, massaged in for about a minute. It absorbs fast and works while you sleep.

settings.question: Will it make my hair greasy?
settings.answer: No. The serum is featherweight and fragrance-free, designed to absorb without residue on your pillow or your morning style.

settings.question: Is it safe for color-treated hair?
settings.answer: Yes. KAMI is applied to the scalp, not the lengths, and plays well with color, keratin, and heat styling.

settings.question: When will I notice a difference?
settings.answer: Hair works on long cycles. Most people notice softness and scalp comfort first, with fuller-looking hair building over consistent nightly use across a few months.

settings.question: Is KAMI a treatment for hair loss?
settings.answer: No. KAMI is a cosmetic serum that supports a healthy-looking scalp and hair. For medical concerns about hair loss, talk with a dermatologist.

settings.question: What is your return policy?
settings.answer: If it's not for you, reach out to our support team within 30 days of delivery and we'll make it right.

settings.headline: Scientific references
settings.intro: Cosmetic ingredient research spans in vitro, animal, and small human studies, and strength varies by ingredient. Peptide data is largely lab-based; the botanical evidence leans on tradition plus emerging studies. Claims on this page are calibrated accordingly.
settings.disclaimer: In-house study statistics are based on our own study; individual results may vary. KAMI is a cosmetic product and is not intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease or medical condition, including hair loss.

settings.title: Copper Tripeptide-1 (GHK-Cu): scalp and follicle support
settings.citations:
Pyo HK, et al. "The effect of tripeptide-copper complex on human hair growth in vitro." Archives of Pharmacal Research, 2007.
Pickart L, Margolina A. "Regenerative and protective actions of the GHK-Cu peptide in the light of the new gene data." International Journal of Molecular Sciences, 2018.

settings.title: Biotinoyl Tripeptide-1: anchoring and thickness appearance
settings.citations: "Evaluation of a peptide-based cosmetic approach to reduce the appearance of hair thinning." Journal of Cosmetic Science; industry-sponsored trials of biotinoyl tripeptide-1 complexes report improved appearance of hair density with topical use. Evidence is early and largely vendor-funded, so claims stay measured.

settings.title: Tsubaki oil (Camellia japonica): shine and conditioning
settings.citations: Reviews of Camellia japonica seed oil document its high oleic-acid lipid profile and traditional Japanese use for hair conditioning and shine; cosmetic evidence is formulation-based rather than clinical.

settings.title: Rice bran (komenuka): scalp conditioning
settings.citations: "Effects of rice bran extract on hair growth in cultured cells and animal models." Published preclinical work suggests rice-bran-derived compounds support the follicle environment; human data is limited, so on-page claims stay cosmetic.

settings.title: Hinoki cypress: scalp freshness
settings.citations: Preclinical studies of hinokitiol (a hinoki-associated compound) report follicle-supportive activity in vitro. Traditional Japanese use centers on scalp cleanliness and comfort.

settings.title: Matcha (EGCG): antioxidant protection
settings.citations:
Kwon OS, et al. "Human hair growth enhancement in vitro by green tea epigallocatechin-3-gallate (EGCG)." Phytomedicine, 2007.
Green tea catechins are widely documented antioxidants; topical evidence for hair is preclinical.
